text: Abd el Krimi has apparently launched a counterstroke to the landing at Allucemus, according to a Madrid communiqué which says that the enemy in the western sector are still obstinately endeavouring to break through the Spanish front in the Penihozimur sector, south of Futuan. General Sons's column offered strong resistance. The conduct of the native troops was especially gallant. The enemy were provided with guns, machine guns and hand grenades.

label: text
text: General Primo de Riveri remains and Tetuan for the present. The communiqué states that reports from Alluenus are very satisfactory. General Sara's troops are consolidating a provisioning base and constructing defence work. The enemy's resistance is slight. The troops under General Fernandes Perez have not yet landed.

text: Speaking at an important meeting of the Council General of the Rhone M. Edmond Herodot said he gave his support to the Government's policy in Morocco. The Council voted unanimously a motion saying that all efforts must be made for the success of the French expedition in Morocco.

text: Salt Lake City, Sept. 10. Mr. Smoot, Chairman of the American Debt Funding Commission, in an address here, declared that France cannot hope for a more favourable settlement of her debt to America than was awarded to Britain. She cannot presume that the United States will accept any plan formulated by the recent conference between Mr. Churchill, British Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Caillaux, French Finance Minister.

text: London, September 10.—The report has been denied that Japanese salvores are preparing to attempt to recover the gold from the Peninsular and Oriental liner Egypt, which sank in May, 1922, off Ushant. On the contrary a French firm is under-taking the work, with German sub-conditioning carrying out the actual diving operations, using a special diving lease for great depth. It is noteworthy that the Egypt carried £1,089,000, of which £830,000 was gold.—Reuter

text: League control in Austria has considerably diminished by the end of the year. League's High Commissioner, Mr. Zimmerman, will leave Vienna in accordance with the Financial Committee's report recommending the gradual abolition of League control, though on Mr. Austen Chamberlain's proposal Australia will undertake not to oppose the reintroduction of control in the event of her failure to fulfil her obligations under the League.

text: A cable dated September 2, stated: — Five men in a disabled seaplane in a rough sea drenched by a tropical storm is the picture evoked by reports of the warships searching in mid-Pacific for seaplane P59, No. 1, one of the two that started to fly to Hawaii. She wirelessed that she would probably be forced to descend at 1.45 p.m. yesterday, 150 knots from the island of Maui, owing to adverse winds and lack of fuel. "We shall crack up if we come down in this weather," was almost the last message received from the plane.

text: Leave of appeal was granted in the Supreme Court yesterday in respect of a case in which Mr. Justice Wood had held against a broker who sued another broker on the grounds that he had broken a contract in not taking up 100 Shanghai Dock shares.

label: text
text: One particular point stressed by Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., who appeared for the petitioner for the appeal, was that Mr. Justice Wood had held for the contract to be binding that an exchange rate for the transaction should be fixed a week before settlement day. The meaning of this term in the contract, said Sir Henry, was that the exchange was to be ascertained one week before settlement day, that was to say the current rate for that day to be ascertained for the purpose of converting itself into Hongkong dollars.

label: text
text: There were other points but he had not been able to get a copy of the judge's notes, said counsel (who was instructed by Mr. G. R. Haywood).

text: From a correspondent who signs himself "J.C." we have received a letter dealing with local problems of the first importance. Owing to the pressure on our space to-day we are unable to publish the letter in full. Referring to the growing atmosphere of "tiredness and drift," J.C. writes:

label: text
text: "There is no excuse for any policy of drift, or for any easing down of our standards as regards the governance of the Colony. In one's wanderings round the city in the course of the day, one seems to notice everywhere a slovenliness and a slackness in the way that public work is being carried on. For example, the streets, before the strike, were always clean and well swept. Now, particularly at tram stops, they look as if they were never swept, or as if the cleaning up and washing away of rubbish depended on the wind and rain. Let one cast one's eyes up the side streets when going along the Praya East on a tram, and notice what a fearful state some of them are in. Not to spin out, what I have said about street cleaning, applies to most of the jobs that are in progress."

label: text
text: "Now let us leave the present and take a long view of the future of Hongkong. Surely by now the Government must have realised the public are not children and that it is quite safe to take them into their confidence as regards the broad outlines of their policy. We all applauded when the rounding up policy was inaugurated, and we can all see what a beneficial effect it has had, particularly in the criminal courts. What we would all like to know—and undoubtedly we are entitled to know—is what the policy is going to be in the future. Are we going to drift back to that miserable policy of admitting the lame, the halt and the blind, the criminals and Bolsheviks, who all make of Hongkong a happy hunting ground? Or are we going to continue the policy of frequent cleanups, followed by the deportation of undesirables? What is the real objection to a poll-tax?"

label: text
text: J.C. points out that the French and Americans are both able to collect a poll tax in neighbouring colonies and suggests that the revenue, amounting to millions even with the poll tax as low as $2 per head, would go a long way to fill “the nasty gap” the depression will make in the Colony's revenue.

label: text
text: "Is one a pessimist if one assumes that British business houses, both old and new, are going to be very badly hit in some cases, perhaps, even to drop out?" J.C. asks next. "Granted that, it means a big reduction of staffs, from top to bottom. One knows, also, that a very large proportion of British coast shipping is laid up, and that Norwegian, Japanese and others have got such a footing that it will be a long time before British shipping is running again at any profit. That means, in conjunction with the starvation wages paid in Norwegian and Japanese ships, that there will be any number of Britishers out of jobs on the China Coast."

label: text
text:
Is it not time that some notice was taken of the increasing numbers of Russians who are flocking into the Colony? There was a time when Russians were forbidden to land here on the ground that Hongkong did not wish to have to face the problem that Shanghai was up against. It is quite time that our own problem of what is going to happen to our own people, who will be axed, during the coming winter, were thoroughly gone into. After pointing to the fact that Russians are doing work which could be done by Britons, J.C. remarks: It is quite time that the Government began to get busy on this problem of unemployment. They have the example of Singapore before them, and there is at present nothing to show that Hongkong may not have to endure just as long and severe a storm as Singapore faced, with practically the same problems.
"Turning to another side of the problem, are the public not entitled to know what the Government are doing to trim ship and shorten sail, to meet the storm? After the recent inquests, with the summings up and the Juries riders, we all know that things in the P.W.D. are pretty rotten. Is the Government going to ignore the suggestion for an expert's inquiry into the working of the P.W.D.? label: text
text: Just two years ago, Mr. L. M. Karukhan was met in Harbin, on his arrival from Moscow, by an enormous crowd of people. He was yesterday greeted by the Soviet citizens's of Harbin in such a manner as Kings and Emperors are accustomed to. A special train of eight cars, including the now celebrated No 56, was sent specially to Chingchun to bring him to Harbin and many representatives of the Russian Consulate and the C. B. R. went to meet him. Thousands of people crowded the roads to the Harbin railway station and literally hundreds of motor cars fought their way through the crowd. As the train steamed into the station, the symphony orchestra played the strains of the "International" and all eyes were fixed on car 56, where, however, only a Russian soldier was to be seen. Mr. Karukhan and suite happened to be in the observation car at the end of the train. As he descended from the curring, the air was rent with motor sirens and horns and the hurrabs of the thousands of people. He entered the large arrival room where fruit and champagne were served and he was introduced to heads of the Railway Departments and to the Chinese administrative chiefs. During this reception the brass band from the Railway Club played selections. After a quarter of an hour, the police made a road for the Soviet ambassador and his family, who entered motor cars and drove to a railway house which has been put at his disposal. Last night a banquet was served at the Chinese Administration quarters, and to-day there are three special fetings to Mr. Karakhan. The first is a lunch at the Railway Workman's Club, the first that this Club has ever given, the second a five o'clock ten at the Railway Club for the hands of all the railway departments and this evening a grand banquet at the Railway Club. To-morrow morning Mr. Karakhan leaves for Moscow, travelling in the special train as far as the frontier and in his special car right through to the end of the journey. The fitting up of this car has cost the C. B. R. a sum of thirty thousand dollars and no crowned head, has ever had such a sumptuous carriage to travel in.
